quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Relative clause verb agrees with a singular antecedent after 'who'
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The employee who ___ the most sales this month will get a bonus.
quests.completedSentence: The employee who makes the most sales this month will get a bonus.
quests.grammarRule: Relative clause verb agrees with a singular antecedent after 'who'
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Who' refers back to 'the employee', which is singular. The verb inside the clause takes -s: 'makes'.
quests.nativeTip: The word right after 'who' refers back to 'the employee' - match the verb to that person.
quests.example: The employee who makes the most sales this month will get a bonus.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Relative clause verb agrees with a singular antecedent after 'who'
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The teacher who ___ this class is very patient.
quests.completedSentence: The teacher who teaches this class is very patient.
quests.grammarRule: Relative clause verb agrees with a singular antecedent after 'who'
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Who' refers to 'the teacher', a singular antecedent, so the verb takes -s: 'teaches'.
quests.nativeTip: 'Who' is standing in for 'the teacher' here - keep the verb singular.
quests.example: The teacher who teaches this class is very patient.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Relative clause verb agrees with a singular antecedent after 'who'
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The scientist who ___ this experiment works alone every night.
quests.completedSentence: The scientist who conducts this experiment works alone every night.
quests.grammarRule: Relative clause verb agrees with a singular antecedent after 'who'
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Who' refers to 'the scientist', which is singular, so the verb takes -s: 'conducts'.
quests.nativeTip: Trace 'who' back to the person it replaces before choosing the verb.
quests.example: The scientist who conducts this experiment works alone every night.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Relative clause verb agrees with a plural antecedent after 'who'
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The employees who ___ overtime get extra pay.
quests.completedSentence: The employees who work overtime get extra pay.
quests.grammarRule: Relative clause verb agrees with a plural antecedent after 'who'
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Who' refers to 'the employees', which is plural, so the verb stays in the base form: 'work'.
quests.nativeTip: This time, 'who' refers back to a plural noun - adjust the verb accordingly.
quests.example: The employees who work overtime get extra pay.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Relative clause verb agrees with a plural antecedent after 'who'
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The students who ___ their homework early have more free time.
quests.completedSentence: The students who finish their homework early have more free time.
quests.grammarRule: Relative clause verb agrees with a plural antecedent after 'who'
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Who' refers to 'the students', a plural antecedent, so the verb stays in the base form: 'finish'.
quests.nativeTip: 'Who' stands in for 'the students' here, which is plural.
quests.example: The students who finish their homework early have more free time.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Relative clause verb agrees with a plural antecedent after 'who'
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The volunteers who ___ at the shelter are always appreciated.
quests.completedSentence: The volunteers who help at the shelter are always appreciated.
quests.grammarRule: Relative clause verb agrees with a plural antecedent after 'who'
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Who' refers to 'the volunteers', which is plural, so the verb stays in the base form: 'help'.
quests.nativeTip: Check the plural noun that 'who' is replacing before choosing the verb.
quests.example: The volunteers who help at the shelter are always appreciated.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Relative clause verb agrees with a singular antecedent after 'which/that'
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The car that ___ in the driveway belongs to my neighbor.
quests.completedSentence: The car that sits in the driveway belongs to my neighbor.
quests.grammarRule: Relative clause verb agrees with a singular antecedent after 'which/that'
quests.ruleExplanation: 'That' refers to 'the car', which is singular, so the verb takes -s: 'sits'.
quests.nativeTip: 'That' can refer to things as well as people - trace it back to find the true antecedent.
quests.example: The car that sits in the driveway belongs to my neighbor.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Relative clause verb agrees with a singular antecedent after 'which/that'
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The recipe which ___ five ingredients is surprisingly easy.
quests.completedSentence: The recipe which requires five ingredients is surprisingly easy.
quests.grammarRule: Relative clause verb agrees with a singular antecedent after 'which/that'
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Which' refers to 'the recipe', which is singular, so the verb takes -s: 'requires'.
quests.nativeTip: 'Which' works the same way as 'that' for agreement - find what it refers to.
quests.example: The recipe which requires five ingredients is surprisingly easy.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Relative clause verb agrees with a singular antecedent after 'which/that'
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The bridge that ___ the two cities was built decades ago.
quests.completedSentence: The bridge that connects the two cities was built decades ago.
quests.grammarRule: Relative clause verb agrees with a singular antecedent after 'which/that'
quests.ruleExplanation: 'That' refers to 'the bridge', which is singular, so the verb takes -s: 'connects'.
quests.nativeTip: Trace 'that' back to the noun it replaces before deciding on the verb.
quests.example: The bridge that connects the two cities was built decades ago.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Relative clause verb agrees with a plural antecedent after 'which/that'
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The books that ___ on this shelf belong to the library.
quests.completedSentence: The books that sit on this shelf belong to the library.
quests.grammarRule: Relative clause verb agrees with a plural antecedent after 'which/that'
quests.ruleExplanation: 'That' refers to 'the books', which is plural, so the verb stays in the base form: 'sit'.
quests.nativeTip: This time, 'that' refers back to a plural noun.
quests.example: The books that sit on this shelf belong to the library.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Relative clause verb agrees with a plural antecedent after 'which/that'
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The machines which ___ in this factory run around the clock.
quests.completedSentence: The machines which operate in this factory run around the clock.
quests.grammarRule: Relative clause verb agrees with a plural antecedent after 'which/that'
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Which' refers to 'the machines', which is plural, so the verb stays in the base form: 'operate'.
quests.nativeTip: 'Which' is standing in for a plural noun here.
quests.example: The machines which operate in this factory run around the clock.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Relative clause verb agrees with a plural antecedent after 'which/that'
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The rules that ___ in this building apply to everyone.
quests.completedSentence: The rules that exist in this building apply to everyone.
quests.grammarRule: Relative clause verb agrees with a plural antecedent after 'which/that'
quests.ruleExplanation: 'That' refers to 'the rules', which is plural, so the verb stays in the base form: 'exist'.
quests.nativeTip: Check whether 'that' is replacing one rule or several before choosing the verb.
quests.example: The rules that exist in this building apply to everyone.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: The main verb agrees with the main subject, not a distractor noun inside the relative clause
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The manager who hires new employees ___ very selective.
quests.completedSentence: The manager who hires new employees is very selective.
quests.grammarRule: The main verb agrees with the main subject, not a distractor noun inside the relative clause
quests.ruleExplanation: The main subject is 'the manager', which is singular; 'employees' (plural) is just inside the relative clause. The main verb takes -s: 'is'.
quests.nativeTip: This blank is outside the relative clause - it needs to agree with the main subject, not the noun inside the clause.
quests.example: The manager who hires new employees is very selective.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: The main verb agrees with the main subject, not a distractor noun inside the relative clause
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The teacher who grades these essays ___ a lot of feedback.
quests.completedSentence: The teacher who grades these essays gives a lot of feedback.
quests.grammarRule: The main verb agrees with the main subject, not a distractor noun inside the relative clause
quests.ruleExplanation: The main subject is 'the teacher', which is singular. The main verb takes -s: 'gives'.
quests.nativeTip: Ignore 'essays' inside the clause and focus on who the sentence is really about.
quests.example: The teacher who grades these essays gives a lot of feedback.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: The main verb agrees with the main subject, not a distractor noun inside the relative clause
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The chef who prepares these dishes ___ years of training.
quests.completedSentence: The chef who prepares these dishes has years of training.
quests.grammarRule: The main verb agrees with the main subject, not a distractor noun inside the relative clause
quests.ruleExplanation: The main subject is 'the chef', which is singular. The main verb takes -s: 'has'.
quests.nativeTip: The plural noun inside the clause doesn't affect the verb that comes after the whole clause.
quests.example: The chef who prepares these dishes has years of training.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: The main verb agrees with the main subject, not a distractor noun inside the relative clause
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The managers who hire new employees ___ very selective.
quests.completedSentence: The managers who hire new employees are very selective.
quests.grammarRule: The main verb agrees with the main subject, not a distractor noun inside the relative clause
quests.ruleExplanation: The main subject is 'the managers', which is plural. The main verb stays in the base form: 'are'.
quests.nativeTip: Compare this to the earlier examples - the main subject here is plural instead of singular.
quests.example: The managers who hire new employees are very selective.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: The main verb agrees with the main subject, not a distractor noun inside the relative clause
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The teachers who grade these essays ___ a lot of feedback.
quests.completedSentence: The teachers who grade these essays give a lot of feedback.
quests.grammarRule: The main verb agrees with the main subject, not a distractor noun inside the relative clause
quests.ruleExplanation: The main subject is 'the teachers', which is plural. The main verb stays in the base form: 'give'.
quests.nativeTip: Focus on the plural main subject, not the noun inside the relative clause.
quests.example: The teachers who grade these essays give a lot of feedback.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: The main verb agrees with the main subject, not a distractor noun inside the relative clause
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The chefs who prepare these dishes ___ years of training.
quests.completedSentence: The chefs who prepare these dishes have years of training.
quests.grammarRule: The main verb agrees with the main subject, not a distractor noun inside the relative clause
quests.ruleExplanation: The main subject is 'the chefs', which is plural. The main verb stays in the base form: 'have'.
quests.nativeTip: As before, the real subject is outside the relative clause, and it's plural here.
quests.example: The chefs who prepare these dishes have years of training.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Relative clause verb agrees with its antecedent, even with a phrase interrupting the clause itself
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The supervisor who, despite a heavy workload, ___ every deadline is highly respected.
quests.completedSentence: The supervisor who, despite a heavy workload, meets every deadline is highly respected.
quests.grammarRule: Relative clause verb agrees with its antecedent, even with a phrase interrupting the clause itself
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Who' refers to 'the supervisor', which is singular, even with 'despite a heavy workload' interrupting the clause. The verb takes -s: 'meets'.
quests.nativeTip: This time, even the relative clause itself has a phrase interrupting it - trace back to the true antecedent.
quests.example: The supervisor who, despite a heavy workload, meets every deadline is highly respected.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Relative clause verb agrees with its antecedent, even with a phrase interrupting the clause itself
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The students who, despite limited resources, ___ excellent results are truly impressive.
quests.completedSentence: The students who, despite limited resources, achieve excellent results are truly impressive.
quests.grammarRule: Relative clause verb agrees with its antecedent, even with a phrase interrupting the clause itself
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Who' refers to 'the students', which is plural, even with the interrupting phrase. The verb stays in the base form: 'achieve'.
quests.nativeTip: Skip over the interrupting phrase inside the clause and find what 'who' refers to.
quests.example: The students who, despite limited resources, achieve excellent results are truly impressive.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Relative clause verb agrees with its antecedent, even with a phrase interrupting the clause itself
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The company that, despite tough competition, ___ strong every year deserves praise.
quests.completedSentence: The company that, despite tough competition, remains strong every year deserves praise.
quests.grammarRule: Relative clause verb agrees with its antecedent, even with a phrase interrupting the clause itself
quests.ruleExplanation: 'That' refers to 'the company', which is singular, even with the interrupting phrase. The verb takes -s: 'remains'.
quests.nativeTip: The interrupting phrase about competition doesn't change what 'that' refers to.
quests.example: The company that, despite tough competition, remains strong every year deserves praise.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Main verb agreement with the true subject, independent of the relative clause
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The book that sits on the top shelf ___ mine.
quests.completedSentence: The book that sits on the top shelf is mine.
quests.grammarRule: Main verb agreement with the true subject, independent of the relative clause
quests.ruleExplanation: The main subject is 'the book', which is singular. The main verb is 'is'.
quests.nativeTip: The relative clause's own verb is already given - focus on the blank outside the clause instead.
quests.example: The book that sits on the top shelf is mine.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Main verb agreement with the true subject, independent of the relative clause
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The workers who arrive early ___ better parking spots.
quests.completedSentence: The workers who arrive early get better parking spots.
quests.grammarRule: Main verb agreement with the true subject, independent of the relative clause
quests.ruleExplanation: The main subject is 'the workers', which is plural. The main verb stays in the base form: 'get'.
quests.nativeTip: Notice the relative clause is already complete - the blank belongs to the main clause.
quests.example: The workers who arrive early get better parking spots.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Main verb agreement with the true subject, independent of the relative clause
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The professor who teaches this course ___ known for tough exams.
quests.completedSentence: The professor who teaches this course is known for tough exams.
quests.grammarRule: Main verb agreement with the true subject, independent of the relative clause
quests.ruleExplanation: The main subject is 'the professor', which is singular. The main verb is 'is'.
quests.nativeTip: Again, look past the completed relative clause to the main subject.
quests.example: The professor who teaches this course is known for tough exams.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Agreement follows the true main subject, even through nested relative clauses with multiple distractor nouns
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The employees who work in the department that handles customer complaints ___ specialized training.
quests.completedSentence: The employees who work in the department that handles customer complaints receive specialized training.
quests.grammarRule: Agreement follows the true main subject, even through nested relative clauses with multiple distractor nouns
quests.ruleExplanation: The true main subject is 'the employees', which is plural, despite the singular 'the department' nested inside the sentence. The verb stays in the base form: 'receive'.
quests.nativeTip: This sentence has two layers of clauses - trace all the way back to the very first noun.
quests.example: The employees who work in the department that handles customer complaints receive specialized training.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Agreement follows the true main subject, even through nested relative clauses with multiple distractor nouns
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The director who oversees the teams that build our software products ___ over a decade of experience.
quests.completedSentence: The director who oversees the teams that build our software products has over a decade of experience.
quests.grammarRule: Agreement follows the true main subject, even through nested relative clauses with multiple distractor nouns
quests.ruleExplanation: The true main subject is 'the director', which is singular, despite the plural nouns nested inside the sentence. The verb takes -s: 'has'.
quests.nativeTip: Even with two clauses stacked together, only the very first noun is the true subject.
quests.example: The director who oversees the teams that build our software products has over a decade of experience.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Agreement follows the true main subject, even through nested relative clauses with multiple distractor nouns
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The reports that were prepared by the analysts who joined last month ___ under review.
quests.completedSentence: The reports that were prepared by the analysts who joined last month remain under review.
quests.grammarRule: Agreement follows the true main subject, even through nested relative clauses with multiple distractor nouns
quests.ruleExplanation: The true main subject is 'the reports', which is plural, despite the singular-sounding details nested inside. The verb stays in the base form: 'remain'.
quests.nativeTip: Trace back past both clauses to find what the sentence is really about.
quests.example: The reports that were prepared by the analysts who joined last month remain under review.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: The main verb agrees with the main subject, not a distractor noun inside the relative clause
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The scientist who published this study ___ well-known in her field.
quests.completedSentence: The scientist who published this study is well-known in her field.
quests.grammarRule: The main verb agrees with the main subject, not a distractor noun inside the relative clause
quests.ruleExplanation: The main subject is 'the scientist', which is singular. The verb is 'is'.
quests.nativeTip: Bring back the basic relative-clause rule: find the main subject outside the clause.
quests.example: The scientist who published this study is well-known in her field.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: The main verb agrees with the main subject, not a distractor noun inside the relative clause
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The employees who requested time off ___ approval from their manager.
quests.completedSentence: The employees who requested time off need approval from their manager.
quests.grammarRule: The main verb agrees with the main subject, not a distractor noun inside the relative clause
quests.ruleExplanation: The main subject is 'the employees', which is plural. The verb stays in the base form: 'need'.
quests.nativeTip: Focus on the plural main subject here, not any noun inside the clause.
quests.example: The employees who requested time off need approval from their manager.

quests.conceptTitle: Grammar Scale: Main verb agreement with the true subject, independent of the relative clause, even with an added interrupting phrase
quests.sentenceWithBlank: The teacher who grades these papers, despite a very busy schedule, ___ detailed comments on each one.
quests.completedSentence: The teacher who grades these papers, despite a very busy schedule, gives detailed comments on each one.
quests.grammarRule: Main verb agreement with the true subject, independent of the relative clause, even with an added interrupting phrase
quests.ruleExplanation: The main subject is 'the teacher', which is singular. The relative clause 'who grades these papers' and the phrase 'despite a very busy schedule' are both extra detail. The main verb takes -s: 'gives'.
quests.nativeTip: As a final check, look past both the relative clause and the interrupting phrase to find the true singular subject.
quests.example: The teacher who grades these papers, despite a very busy schedule, gives detailed comments on each one.
